title: Instance-Based vs Model-Based Learning
abstract:
Two fundamentally different answers to the question what does a trained
model actually contain? An instance-based learner keeps the training data and
compares; a model-based learner distils the data into parameters and throws the
data away. This document covers both philosophies, what each stores, where each
spends its compute, how each generalises, the decision surfaces they produce,
and why the distinction dictates whether your model can run on a phone.

blocks.t: The Question Being Answered
The framing

These two terms describe how a model learns — by remembering
data directly, or by learning a general rule from it.
Ask a trained model: "what are you, physically, on disk?"

items: An instance-based learner answers: "I am the training set."
A model-based learner answers: "I am a handful of numbers."

blocks.cap:
The concrete difference. Train both on 10{,}000 rows: KNN's artefact
 is 10{,}000 rows; logistic regression's artefact is three numbers.

blocks.t: Instance-Based Learning
The one-sentence version

Makes a prediction by comparing new data to stored training examples.
The idea is "Remember & Compare".

There is no genuine "training" phase. Fitting means storing. All the
work happens at prediction time: the model looks up which stored examples the
query resembles and answers accordingly.
The canonical example: K-Nearest Neighbours
A new point is classified based on the labels of the nearest points.

items: Compute the distance from $x_q$ to every stored row.

Classification: majority vote among their labels.
 Regression: mean of their targets.

blocks.t: Stated formally

Let $N_k(x_q)$ be the indices of the $k$ training points closest to $x_q$ under
a distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ — usually Euclidean,
d(x_q,x_i)=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left(x_{qj}-x_{ij}\right)^2}.
Then

\hat y_{\text{cls}}(x_q)=\operatorname*{arg max}_{c} \sum_{i\in N_k(x_q)} \mathbb{1}[y_i=c],
 \qquad
 \hat y_{\text{reg}}(x_q)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in N_k(x_q)} y_i .

Notice that no parameters appear anywhere. There is nothing to estimate.
The training data itself plays the role that $w$ plays in a linear model. This is
why instance-based methods are also called non-parametric and
lazy learners.
Why "lazy"}

The learner postpones all generalisation until a query arrives. It never forms
a global hypothesis about the data — it forms a local one, freshly, for
each query. This is also called memory-based or analogical
learning.

Other instance-based methods: kernel density estimation, locally weighted
regression (LOWESS), case-based reasoning systems, and — in a real sense —
the retrieval step of a RAG pipeline.
Model-Based Learning
The one-sentence version

Learns rules/parameters from the data and then uses them for
prediction. The data is a means; the parameters are the product.

Training is a genuine optimisation: you posit a functional form, define a loss,
and search for the parameters that minimise it. Afterwards the training data is
no longer needed and can be deleted.
Stated formally
Choose a parametric family $f_\theta$ and solve

\hat\theta=\operatorname*{arg min}_{\theta} \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}
 L \left(f_\theta(x_i),y_i\right)+\lambda\Omega(\theta).

Prediction is then $\hat y = f_{\hat\theta}(x_q)$ — an $O(p)$ arithmetic
expression, independent of $n$. The $n$ training rows have been compressed
into $\dim(\theta)$ numbers.

Examples: linear regression ($y=mx+c$ — store $m$ and $c$), logistic
regression, SVM (store the support vectors and the dual coefficients), decision
trees (store the split thresholds), neural networks (store the weight matrices),
Naive Bayes (store the class-conditional probabilities).
Why "eager"

The learner does all its generalising up front, before any query exists.
It commits to one global hypothesis about how the world works. Also called
parametric learning, because the number of parameters is fixed in
advance and does not grow with $n$.
What the Two Philosophies Produce

blocks.cap:
Decision surfaces on identical data. KNN with $k=1$ carves an
 irregular surface that honours every single training point, including the
 noisy ones — it has memorised. As $k$ grows the surface smooths. Logistic
 regression cannot produce anything but a straight line, no matter what the
 data does; its hypothesis space is that restricted.

blocks.t: The bias–variance reading of this picture
This is the bias–variance tradeoff (Topic 40) made visible.

items:
$k=1$ KNN: low bias, high variance. It assumes almost nothing
 about the shape of the truth, so it fits anything — including the noise.

Logistic regression: high bias, low variance. It assumes the
 boundary is linear. If that assumption is wrong it will never recover,
 but it is extremely stable across different training samples.

$k=15$ KNN sits between them. $k$ is the dial: small $k$ $\to$
 overfitting, large $k$ $\to$ underfitting.

blocks.t: Where the Compute Goes

blocks.cap:
Measured on real runs. KNN's "training" is essentially free and its
 prediction cost grows with the training-set size. Logistic regression pays once
 during fitting and then predicts in constant time forever. Note the log scale.

blocks.t: Complexity
With $n$ training rows, $p$ features, $m$ queries:

Tree-based indices (KD-tree, ball tree) reduce the prediction term to roughly
$O(p\log n)$ in low dimensions — but they degrade to brute force once $p$ grows
past roughly 20, which is the curse of dimensionality biting (Topic 32).
The deployment consequence

An instance-based model cannot be shipped to a phone if the training set
is 40 GB, and its latency grows as your dataset grows — exactly the wrong
scaling for a successful product. A model-based artefact is a few kilobytes and
answers in microseconds regardless of how much data trained it. This single
consideration decides many real architecture debates.
Full Comparison

head: Dimension
Instance-based
Model-based
rows: Severely — distance is the whole method
Varies; gradient methods yes, trees no
KNN, kernel density estimation, LOWESS, case-based reasoning
logistic regression, decision trees, SVM, Naive Bayes, neural networks

\caption{The tradeoff is not "which is better" — it is where you want to
pay.}

blocks.t: The blurry cases worth knowing

SVM is model-based but stores the support vectors — actual
training points. It is a hybrid: parametric in the dual, instance-flavoured in
what it retains.
Random forests are model-based, but a tree's leaf is effectively a
memorised region of training points.
Gaussian processes are fully non-parametric and keep the whole training
set, exactly like KNN. The dichotomy is a useful axis, not a hard partition.
Code

import numpy as np, time, pickle
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (20_000, 20))
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.6 * X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
Xq = rng.normal(0, 1, (2_000, 20))

# =====================================================================
# INSTANCE-BASED -- "training" is just memorisation
# =====================================================================
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
t = time.perf_counter(); knn.fit(X, y);      t_fit_knn  = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); knn.predict(Xq);    t_pred_knn = time.perf_counter() - t

# Proof that the model IS the data:
print("KNN stores the training matrix:", knn._fit_X.shape)   # (20000, 20)
print("KNN artefact size:", len(pickle.dumps(knn)), "bytes") # ~3 MB

# =====================================================================
# MODEL-BASED -- training compresses, prediction is arithmetic
# =====================================================================
lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
t = time.perf_counter(); lr.fit(X, y);       t_fit_lr  = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); lr.predict(Xq);     t_pred_lr = time.perf_counter() - t

print("LogReg stores only:", lr.coef_.shape, lr.intercept_.shape)  # (1,20) (1,)
print("LogReg artefact size:", len(pickle.dumps(lr)), "bytes")     # ~1 KB

print(f"fit  : knn {t_fit_knn:.4f}s   logreg {t_fit_lr:.4f}s")
print(f"pred : knn {t_pred_knn:.4f}s   logreg {t_pred_lr:.4f}s")
# Typical output: KNN fits ~500x faster and predicts ~200x slower.


# =====================================================================
# KNN FROM SCRATCH -- to show there is no "learning" at all
# =====================================================================
class MyKNN:
    def __init__(self, k=5):
        self.k = k

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = X, y      # <-- the ENTIRE "training" procedure
        return self

    def predict(self, Xq):
        # squared Euclidean distance from every query to every stored row
        d2 = ((Xq[:, None, :] - self.X[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)
        idx = np.argpartition(d2, self.k, axis=1)[:, :self.k]   # k nearest
        votes = self.y[idx]                                     # their labels
        return (votes.mean(axis=1) >= 0.5).astype(int)          # majority vote

print("scratch KNN matches sklearn:",
      (MyKNN(5).fit(X, y).predict(Xq[:200]) == knn.predict(Xq[:200])).mean())


# =====================================================================
# WHY SCALING IS NON-NEGOTIABLE FOR INSTANCE-BASED METHODS
# =====================================================================
# age is O(10), salary is O(100000) -> salary alone decides every distance
Xs = np.c_[rng.uniform(20, 60, 3000), rng.uniform(20_000, 200_000, 3000)]
ys = (Xs[:, 0] > 40).astype(int)          # the TRUTH depends only on age

raw    = KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(Xs[:2000], ys[:2000])
scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5)).fit(Xs[:2000], ys[:2000])
print("KNN unscaled accuracy:", raw.score(Xs[2000:], ys[2000:]))     # ~0.55
print("KNN scaled   accuracy:", scaled.score(Xs[2000:], ys[2000:]))  # ~0.97

# A decision tree is unaffected -- it splits per feature, never combines them:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
print("Tree unscaled accuracy:",
      DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3).fit(Xs[:2000], ys[:2000]).score(Xs[2000:], ys[2000:]))


# =====================================================================
# ADDING NEW DATA -- the operational difference
# =====================================================================
Xnew, ynew = rng.normal(0, 1, (100, 20)), rng.integers(0, 2, 100)

# instance-based: append. done. O(1).
knn.fit(np.vstack([X, Xnew]), np.r_[y, ynew])

# model-based: the parameters must be re-solved from scratch.
lr.fit(np.vstack([X, Xnew]), np.r_[y, ynew])
Choosing Between Them

head: Reach for instance-based when
Reach for model-based when
rows: The dataset is small and low-dimensional
The dataset is large or high-dimensional
The decision boundary is complex and irregular
You cannot posit a functional form
You need a small deployable artefact
Data arrives constantly and retraining is expensive
You must explain the model to a regulator
You want "show me similar past cases" as the explanation
You want to extrapolate beyond the training range

blocks.t: Extrapolation: the failure mode that surprises people

KNN cannot extrapolate. Its prediction is always an average of stored
targets, so it is mathematically incapable of returning a value outside the
range of the training targets. Ask it to price a house twice the size of anything
it has seen and it will return the price of the biggest house it knows. A linear
model will happily extrapolate — sometimes correctly, sometimes absurdly, but
it will at least respond to the input.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
The distinction is how a model learns: by remembering data
 directly, or by learning a general rule from it.

Instance-based = Remember & Compare. Stores the training
 set; predicts by comparing a query to it. Example: KNN. Also
 called lazy / non-parametric.

Model-based = learns rules or parameters from the data and
 uses them to predict. Examples: linear regression, decision
 trees, SVM, neural networks. Also called eager / parametric.

Instance-based: training free, prediction expensive, memory grows with
 $n$, no extrapolation, brutally sensitive to feature scaling and
 irrelevant features.

Model-based: training expensive, prediction constant-time, tiny artefact,
 restricted hypothesis space (that restriction is its bias).

The cost is not eliminated — it is moved between train time and
 predict time. Choose based on where your system can afford to pay.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why is KNN called a lazy learner?

Because it does no generalisation at fit time — fit() only stores the
data. All the work is deferred to prediction, where it forms a fresh local
hypothesis for each query.

Q. Which is better for a real-time API serving 10{,}000 requests per
second?

Model-based, decisively. KNN's per-query cost scales with the training-set size,
so latency degrades as your data grows. A logistic regression or gradient-boosted
tree answers in microseconds from a fixed-size artefact.
Q. Does KNN need feature scaling? Does a decision tree?

KNN: absolutely — it computes distances, so a feature measured in hundreds of
thousands drowns out one measured in tens. Decision trees: no — they threshold
one feature at a time and never combine features into a distance, so any
monotone rescaling leaves the tree unchanged.
Q. Can KNN predict a value it has never seen?

No, not for regression. Its output is an average of stored targets, so it is
bounded by the observed target range. It cannot extrapolate.
Q. Is a decision tree parametric or non-parametric?

Non-parametric in the strict sense — the number of nodes is not fixed in
advance and grows with the data — but it is model-based, because it
stores learned split rules rather than the training rows. This is why
"parametric" and "model-based" are not perfect synonyms.
Q. Where do you see instance-based learning in modern systems?

Vector databases and RAG. Embedding a query and retrieving the nearest stored
documents is precisely KNN with a learned distance metric — instance-based
learning at the centre of the current AI stack.
